1.	Course Description: 
Supply Chain Management (SCM) is a cross-functional discipline concerned with the movement of products, the use of business resources, the flow of information, and the deployment of services in the value chain. In this introductory course, students are provided with a comprehensive overview of the business processes, value-creating activities, and best practices for managing a supply chain.

2.	Learning Objectives 
(1)	Provide a comprehensive overview of SCM-related business processes and problems and pinpoint the strategic role of SCM and relationship to other business disciplines. 
(2)	Equip students with SCM best practices and related basic analytical models/tools. 
(3)	Provide a roadmap to more specialized courses on SCM-related topics.
3.	Learning outcomes

1)	Students will understand the main processes and common challenges in supply chain management and how SCM integrates with other business functions.
2)	Students will be able to identify and apply best practices and basic analytical tools to solve supply chain management problems effectively.
3)	Students will have a foundational understanding that prepares them for more specialized courses and career development in supply chain management.

Course Description:
Managing personal finances and wealth is the key for the successful and stress life of an
individual. This course helps the students to make informed financial decisions in their
life by reducing the risk of ending in financial turmoil. This course aims to provide a
strong foundation for managing personal finance and wealth of students through real-
world applications, case studies, and interactive activities. Students will develop the
knowledge and confidence to achieve financial stability and growth.
Learning Objectives:
Students will develop practical skills in budgeting, saving, and investing, while also
gaining an understanding of credit management, tax planning, and retirement
strategies. By exploring various financial instruments available and equip them to
optimize their wealth-building efforts and achieve financial security. The course also
emphasizes the importance of risk management, financial psychology, and consumer
protection, ensuring that students can navigate financial challenges with confidence.
Ultimately, the course aims to cultivate responsible financial habits and long-term
wealth management strategies for a secure and prosperous future.

Learning Outcomes:

After completing this course, the participants should be able to:
1) Students will be able to learn how to prepare and manage the personal budget viz.,
expenses, savings effectively.
2) Students will get an overview of investment options available to build their wealth.
3) Students will learn how to plan financially for their higher education, home loan,
retirement, health and Insurance.
4) Students learn on assessing financial risks, recognize fraudulent schemes, and build
strategies for secures future.

The course aims to give students a comprehensive understanding of portfolio
management principles, including constructing and evaluating portfolios.
Topics we cover include the market indices, efficiency frontier, the Markowitz portfolio,
capital asset pricing, model, arbitrage pricing theory, factor models, active and passive
investing, smart beta, beta core, bucket investment, simulation, optimization, Sharpe
ratio, Traynor ratio, Mutual funds etc.
Learning Objectives:
1. Understand risk and return
2. History of stock returns
3. Market efficiency
4. Risk return relationship
5. Construct and evaluate portfolios

Ever since the introduction of Bitcoin in 2008, Cryptocurrencies and the Blockchain technology
have become very popular contributing to a lot of excitement and hype in business circles. While
crypto-currencies have not been welcomed warmly, especially by the regulators, the usefulness
of Blockchain, the technology underpinning Bitcoin has been universally recognized 1 (even by
detractors of cryptocurrencies). Increasingly, Blockchain technology is finding applications
outside the Fintech industry including areas such as Supply chain management, fraud detection,
health, agriculture, education, government and the like. With this kind of proliferation, it is not
inconceivable that present and future managers will encounter Blockchain in some form sooner
rather than later.
This course intends to equip student, the present and future managers, with relevant and working
knowledge of Cryptocurrencies and the Blockchain technology. Blockchain, a potentially
disruptive technology has various known and potentially useful applications across various
industry verticals.
Course Objectives:

The main objective of this course is to equip students with an understanding of the emerging
technology of blockchain that will enable them to:
- Assess the applicability of Blockchain technology and its business benefits in business
contexts that are characterized by “trust” mechanisms.
- Understand the interaction between different Blockchain components.
- Where and how to implement Blockchain
- Design innovative Blockchain Applications

column6: Capital Markets - Trading, Analysis and Investment Strategy
column22:
This dynamic capital markets course transforms students from market observers to informed investors through hands-on trading simulations, real-time market analysis, and portfolio management. Students will navigate the complexities of stock markets, bond markets,
derivatives, and alternative investments while building practical skills in financial analysis, risk assessment, and investment strategy. The course culminates in a Portfolio Management Competition where students present their investment strategies to a panel.
Learning Objectives:
1. Understand the structure and functioning of global capital markets
2. Master fundamental and technical analysis techniques for investment decisions
3. Develop practical skills in portfolio construction and risk management
4. Gain hands-on experience with trading platforms and financial data analysis
5. Learn to evaluate and present investment strategies effectively

Economists primarily use mathematical methods to make and study economic arguments. Mathematics brings in the rigour and precision that are required to ensure that the economists’ statements are true and logically sound. This course is intended to familiarize students with mathematical concepts and methods typically used by economists, and introduce ideas from topics in differential and integral calculus, optimization, linear algebra, and financial economics. A course in these topics will lay the foundation for more rigorous courses in (various branches of) economic theory, statistics and econometrics.
 
 The goal of the course is not to delve into the theorem-proof route, but rather to help the students develop their mathematical reasoning and intuition, and become comfortable talking about economics using mathematical shorthand.

column22:
This course has a dual focus: First, to introduce you to probability theory and the basic statistical concepts that are used to explore and understand economic phenomena. Second, to show you how this statistical knowledge can be applied to real world data using widely available spreadsheet tools like Microsoft Excel. Therefore, this course has been designed very much from a practitioner’s point of view. You will find that the material that you learn in this course will have direct application in your jobs and further studies. Sound grasp of material from this course will also be essential for your further coursework in econometrics and advanced microeconomics.
 
 The topics covered in this course fall into three broad categories: descriptive statistics, probability & distributions, and hypothesis testing. Descriptive statistics deals with the visualization and summarization of statistical data. You will learn simple tools for visualizing data on one and two variables, as well as statistical concepts for summarizing the central location and dispersion of your data. In the probability & distributions section, you will learn about probability and surrounding concepts like sample spaces, random variables, and combinatorics. You will also learn about some common discrete and continuous probability distributions. Hypothesis testing deals with questions of statistical inference: when are our conditions supported by the data and when are they not? You will learn about samples, and populations, point and interval estimates, and the apparatus of hypothesis testing about one or two variables.

This course is aimed at introducing economics students to statistical programming, using R and Stata. In this course, students will learn the basics of programming – such as downloading and installing the programme(s), managing libraries and packages, and good coding practices. Students will learn to perform simple computations, including basic mathematical operations, creating vectors and variables, and working with frequently used tools such as conditionals and loops. 
 
 Through a combination of lectures, hands-on exercises, and projects, students will be exposed to different data structures, and learn the tools to manipulate and analyse data – importing data from different sources/in various formats, and transforming them into a format suitable for analysis, cleaning data and dealing with missing information, and data visualization/description – creating and formatting charts and tables. Based on students’ comfort level with these foundational skills, the course may also touch upon additional topics related to simple statistical tests and analyses.

It introduces students to several families of distributions and explores commonly used empirical approaches to identify causality. The course also features advanced topics such as instrumental variable estimation, panel data models, and limited dependent variables. At the end of this course, students should be able to have a deeper appreciation for the link between theory and empirical work, and also be able to engage meaningfully with current empirical literature in economics.

column22: This course is a sequel to Microeconomics II specially designed for the students enrolled in the FYUP. It will focus on the study of market failure under second best settings. It will also dwell deeper into game theory, public goods, factor markets, and time costs. The concept of the market equilibrium will be re-introduced, and we will learn how the characteristics of the market vary in the real word leading to conditions such that market fails to achieve an equilibrium, focusing on externalities, public goods, markets with asymmetric information and imperfect competition. The course would develop a rigorous set of tools to analyze such conditions while unraveling how choices can interact and persist leading to strategic outcomes and payoffs.

column22: Economics, like other disciplines, claims a rich history shaped by historical, societal, economic, and political contexts. In this course, we explore how economic ideas evolve over time, influenced by changing political and societal values and needs. By understanding the historical roots of economic theories, we try to gain insight into the development of current dominant ideas. This course aims to equip undergraduate students with a nuanced understanding of the historical development of the great ideas of economic thought and its implications for addressing contemporary economic challenges.

column22:
Since Adam Smith and David Ricardo, economists have sought to understand the causes, patterns, and consequences of trade among nations. This course introduces students to the key concepts, theories, institutions, and macroeconomic dynamics of international economics. It traces the historical evolution of the global trading system - from Mercantilism and the Gold Standard through Bretton Woods, GATT, and the WTO - and examines why countries trade, what they trade, who gains, and how governments shape trade through policy. Students will engage with the principal theories of trade (Absolute and Comparative Advantage, Heckscher-Ohlin, economies of scale and imperfect competition) and evaluate trade policy instruments including tariffs, quotas, subsidies, anti-dumping measures, and non-tariff barriers.
The course also covers the monetary dimensions of international economics: exchange rate regimes (fixed, floating, managed, pegged, spot, forward, and trade-weighted), balance of payments accounting, capital account convertibility, and global capital flows, analyzed through open-economy frameworks including the IS-LM-BOP model. Historical episodes - the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, the oil shocks of the 1970s, the rise of the US dollar as reserve currency - provide context for contemporary debates around the US-China trade conflict, Trump-era tariffs, supply chain disruptions, economic nationalism, industrial policy, digital and services trade, climate-related trade measures, and the geopolitics of regional agreements and groupings such as the QUAD. The course equips students with the analytical tools to navigate the rapidly changing landscape of global economic relations.

column6: Economics Through Games (Formerly know as "Game Theory - ECON327")
column22: Game theory studies interactive decision-making and our objective is to understand the impact of interactions of multiple players and the resulting dynamics in a market environment. The introductory course in game theory will familiarize students with strategic behaviour and its applications in business decision making and several fields such as industrial organization, corporate finance, environmental economics, trade and political science. The course will cover several solution concepts starting with Nash Equilibrium, which will be modified under imperfect and incomplete/complete information scenarios. The concepts will be applied to case studies in bargaining, negotiation, pricing and market entry decisions.

Labor economics, in a comprehensive sense, involves examining how individuals, firms, institutions, and the public sector interact to influence employment and wage outcomes. Throughout this course, we will delve into both theoretical and empirical aspects of labor economics, placing a significant emphasis on practical applications. We will focus on discussing research designs aimed at empirically measuring theoretical predictions and assessing the impact of policy interventions.

column6: Themes in Economic history: Humans as Planetary Pilots
column22: This course intends to explain economic events and phenomena in their historical contexts, recognizing such thinking to be central to the discipline of economics itself. As such, this course reinforces the idea that history and economics are inextricably linked. By taking a global approach, this course seeks to address and engage fundamental questions concerning the emergence of the modern world economy, the origins of sustained economic growth, the economic divergence between the so-called East and the West, widening of the gap between the rich and the poor in terms of both individuals and nations and major challenges confronting modern societies today and beyond. In so doing, we will understand (a) how technologies, institutions and innovations spurred and continue to spur economic growth and (b) how wealth generated thus is redistributed. This course has two core objectives: first, to present a general introduction to global economic history by examining how trade, geography, labor, and technology shaped and remade human cultures since the Neolithic Revolution; second, to explore specific topics in relation to modern economies since the Industrial Revolution.

column6: From Mughaliyah Saltanat to Sovereign Republic: India in Transition
column22: This course will study the processes that transformed India from a Mughal Empire to a Sovereign Republic. Until 1857 the Mughal emperor remained the fount of political legitimacy of South Asia even as the actual power of the Mughals waned. Mughal successor states including Awadh, Hyderabad, Bengal and even the British East India Company at least nominally drew their authority from the Mughal crown. By 1950 India had emerged as a republic whose rulers derived legitimacy from democratic elections. This course concerns itself with an overarching question of great importance to both political scientists and historians. How did conceptions of sovereignty in South Asia shift as a consequence of colonialism?

column6: Food and Power (formerly Reading Food, Understanding Identities)

column22:
To eat, like breathing, is a biological instinct of our bodies, necessary for daily functioning. Unlike breathing however, the ways in which we eat, the food items we choose or reject, are linked to societal norms and economic capacities, beyond individual agency. This course will read foodways as systems of communications that encode identities in terms of state and household institutions, geographical markers, religious affiliations, labour and class positions, and caste and gender norms.

This course will move chronologically through the turn to agriculture, ancient states and empires, religious sacrifices and asceticism, medieval mercantilism, industrialisation and circulation of food and labour, and end in the present day post-globalisation world. We will learn to read primary sources ranging from the pots and pans of the ancient world, medicinal texts, religious canonical literature, oral and written recipe collections, and modern day popular culture. Together, we will use these contexts and sources to understand how food functions as a marker of identity.

This course aims to introduce students to the foundational principles of acquiring knowledge in Indian philosophy. Indian epistemology covers the nature of knowledge (jñāna), the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the criteria of valid knowledge (pramā). This course deals with two major schools – the Nyāya philosophy and the Buddhist philosophy – which have built the foundation of what is known as Indian epistemology. While briefly introducing major Indian philosophical schools, it will focus on these two and learn about their major texts and thinkers. We will briefly touch upon the points of debate between both the schools.

We will be reading an excerpt (i.e., from statement 34 to 54) of the Tarkasaṅgraha for understanding epistemology of Nyāya. Written by Annambhaṭṭa, this is a concise text which presents the ontology and the epistemology of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika systems. For understanding Buddhist epistemology, we will be reading the first chapter (direct perception) of the Nyāyabindu. This is a short treatise by Dharmakīrti, one of the most influential philosophers of Buddhist epistemology. Since this is an introductory course, we will only be reading the texts in translation and not their extensive commentaries. This course will familiarize students with the primary texts of Indian epistemology and will give them a glimpse of the significance it holds in the larger philosophical domain. This course also paves the way for studying ontology and metaphysics in Indian philosophy.

column6: Pre-Socratics and the Socratics - History of Philosophy
column22:
This course will introduce students to thinkers who collectively formed the philosophical tradition of the ancient Greece. It will first familiarize students to the philosophical thoughts of
the pre-Socratic thinkers like Thales, Pythagoras, Parmenides, Heraclitus and Democritus. Then, the focus of the course will shift to Socrates, and the two major Socratic philosophers – Plato and Aristotle. Students will be introduced to the ethical and metaphysical concerns of these three thinkers through the selected works of Plato and Aristotle. Philosophical themes including moral virtues (like justice, wisdom, piety etc.), good, beauty, happiness, death, God and soul will be explored in these classes. Taking a historical approach, the course will enable students to systematically and critically reflect on specific philosophical issues that were relevant to the ancient Greeks.

column6: Reason and Experience and the Foundations of Modern Western Epistemology
column22: This course will take up a discussion on the epistemological views of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, David Hume, and Immanuel Kant. These are three canonical thinkers in the Modern Western radition, whose writings discuss the relations between reason and experience, which is  fundamental to understanding modern estern epistemological thought. The objective of the course is to take the students through a discussion of the primary texts (i) in order to locate the dominant trends in modern western thought through their writings, and (ii) to do a close reading of the texts, and see how, they as independent thinkers, challenge or conform to the dominant trends. The course restricts itself to reading Leibniz, Hume and Kant, as these thinkers are typically characterised as a rationalist thinker, an empiricist thinker, and as someone who brings together rationalism and empiricism, respectively.

Aesthetics is an integral philosophical enquiry which is deeply concerned with our experience of the world and our perception of it. This course will introduce the students to basic concepts in aesthetics and with a focus on the various kinds of aesthetic practices and their entanglement with socio-political, geographical, historical contexts as well as the larger philosophical debates around aesthetics. Concepts of sense perception, beauty, taste, judgment and poetics will be discussed based on core readings including Aristotle, Abhinavagupta, Kant, Bourdieu, Kumaraswamy, and others. A foundational understanding of aesthetics gives students a philosophical grounding in approaching any form of literature and art with the relevant vocabulary and conceptual frame of reference. This will enable students to pursue their interests in engaging with the arts in any way forward - through theory or practice.
column24: This course is required for Litt & Arts major ARTS208|LITT209

column22: The ‘Image’ is a powerful concept that fuels foundational discourses in philosophy of art. The phenomenologists were captivated by the image and what it could tell us. From the practices of creating death masks, to painting, to capturing, to making images move, to projecting images still and moving, the fascination with alterity underlines much of the aesthetics of modernity. In this course, we shall particularly focus on three European philosophers who have extensively theorized on the image – Jacques Ranciere, Gilles Deleuze and Villem Flusser with minor detours into the phenomenological ruminations by Sartre and Husserl. The course will be reading intensive and will engage with works of art in conversation with the readings prescribed.

This course offers a critical introduction to the evolution and practice of democratic politics in India, with a focus on the postcolonial state and its institutions. Through a thematic exploration of the Indian state, constitutional vision, institutional frameworks, and contemporary political challenges, students will gain a grounded understanding of how democracy was imagined, built, and contested in India.
Beginning with philosophical and historical reflections on the idea of the state, the course situates the Indian experience within broader traditions of political thought. It then traces how India's Constitution emerged as a blueprint for reconciling diversity with unity, exploring foundational principles such as federalism, secularism, and social justice. The course examines how these ideals were institutionalized through the Parliament, Judiciary, and Election Commission—and how they have evolved in response to changing political contexts, including the rise of majoritarianism, debates on federalism under the Modi government, and policies like "One Nation, One Election."
Emphasizing both historical depth and contemporary relevance, the course interrogates how India’s democratic project has negotiated its plural society marked by caste, religion, language, and regional identities. Through key political episodes—such as the Emergency, Mandal vs. Kamandal, and hijab and language debates—students will explore tensions between liberty and order, rights and identity, and state power and popular resistance. Engaging with primary texts, constitutional debates, and critical scholarship, the course encourages students to think analytically about the Indian state and its evolving role in shaping democratic citizenship.

In broad continuity with the course Introduction to Comparative Politics, this course involves a deeper engagement with the key themes and methodological approaches that constitute the dynamic field of Comparative Politics. This course offers an advanced exploration of conceptual variables such as state formation and state capacity, social movements, and civil society as well as ideologically conditioned political processes such as democratisation, and development across supra-national, national, and local levels. The thematic composition of this course is informed by gender and intersectional lenses. Beginning with the evolution of the field beyond its Euro-American moorings, the course will delve into the diverse methods that characterise comparative research. This is followed by a historically contextualised study of dominant political ideologies. Other key themes covered in the course include political parties, representative democracy, and contemporary phenomena such as populism.

column6: Politics in Multiple Frames: Approaches, concepts and theoretical perspectives
column22: This course seeks to outline various perspectives of understanding politics at multiple levels from the local to the national to the global. Is politics essentially about power, government and elections, or is it about friends and foes? Could it be about a deep yet contested conversation about public goods or an art of bringing political differences into an integral but tension-ridden whole? Students will develop a foundational understanding of historical, empirical and normative dimensions of politics at each of these scales. What are the pressing questions that we encounter at different levels of politics, and how did the systems that organise them come to be, and what are the epistemologies and power dynamics that underpin them? How does the academic discipline of politics constitute its objects of study and protocols of enquiry? Can the focus of politics be exclusively on human action, and such a focus be sustained in times of deep ecological crises?

The study of politics is much more than the study of the state. It involves the examination and engagement with the social and political structures, concepts, ideas and values. Thus, concepts like equality, liberty, rights, justice, sovereignty, power, democracy, modernity, nationalism, identity, state, legitimacy and dissent become central to the discipline of politics. Political Theory I exposes the students to some of these concepts. However, the course on Political Theory II will engage with the remaining concepts through the ongoing debates around some of the concepts like sovereignty, power, nationalism, democracy, identity and modernity. The engagement with these debates bring to the surface how certain concepts complicate or simplify the understanding and applicability of other concepts in a polity. The engagement with these concepts manifests in political action. Political action aims at either preservation or change guided by the thought of better or worse. This is deeply embedded in finding the good or the right driven by what starts as a question and ends with knowledge. Thus, political theory is driven towards the pursuit of knowledge for the good of society, polity, people and collectives exhibited in the establishment of order and resolution of contestation or conflict. The engagements with ongoing debates enhances this pursuit of knowledge which is deeply embedded in explanatory wisdom for the truth. Thus, the course will engage with such a quest for knowledge while resolving ongoing contestations, conflicts and debates that aim at generating consent and acceptance for an ordered polity. The course will be anchored to the challenges to state and sovereignty, contestations over power and legitimacy, debate around dissent safeguarding democracy or democracy being dissent, paradox of modernity and identity and the elusiveness of nationalism. It is through a critical engagement and coherent analysis of the concepts and the ongoing debates and challenges around them that the course will enrich political theory and the discipline of politics as it will create the knowledge of the whole by putting the parts together.
column23: POLT313 | SOCL313 | PHIL313 Introduction to Political Theory: Concepts and Conundrums

column6: Social and Political Thought: Intimations of Modernity
column22: This course deals with ideas articulated by individual thinkers such as Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Weber and Marx on society, politics, and power. In addition, it covers different ways of thinking of ‘past’, their attendant imaginaries, and the politics of identity and recognition in the modern world.  Both these parts are connected by and anchored in the stories of ‘modernity’. ‘Modernity’ is a large  and complex theme that encompasses transformations in the sphere of economy, politics, society and  morals. It does not offer a unitary story. We also know that it has become a global currency for  justifying as well as critiquing power. Separated by a long stretch of time, how do we make sense of  these ideas? How these thinkers, spanning a period of four centuries, were not only shaped by  significant sociopolitical changes but also created new ways of comprehending them? The course  brings interpretive and methodological resources from sociological theories, political philosophy, and historical imagination to examine ideas and experiences that define ‘modern’ life and their embattled presence in our time

The socio-cultural construction of the body is intrinsic to the constitution of the self. The body does not just define the ‘self’ but also the ‘other’ or ‘non-self’. The body is a source of knowledge while understanding social positioning and is understood through everyday living. Beauty is closely connected to the body. It is defined in terms of the perfect body and bodily appearances. In fact societies have been obsessed with a beautiful body for long. The body is a strong communicator and has a specific political anatomy of its own. It can see and is also constantly seen by the others. The course will look at the body from a political perspective and navigate through questions like what constitutes the body and how we see them. It will help in understanding the process of othering that constantly takes place in the socio-economic-political-cultural milieu we inhabit. By taking the body as the source of intervention, the course will engage with questions of self, identity, subjectivity and objectification. Thus, engaging with the sociological construction of the body, politics of visibility or that of seeing and be seen, heightened presence of technology, bodies as embodiment of caste, religion, space and disability becomes unavoidable and pivotal. It opens up the domain of alternative narratives that make us look at the body as made up of a plurality and multiplicity of bodies. The course will draw from articulations and conversations that have already been initiated by scholars like Judith Butler, Michel Foucault, Erving Goffman, Bryan Turner etc to enrich the discourse on body politics.

This course is designed as an analytical, contextualised introduction to Indian foreign policy and strategic thinking. The course is designed to enable students to follow contemporary debates in an informed and critical way, and from multiple points of view. Traditionally, this topic is taught through a historical approach and an overview of bilateral relationships. This course will merge that with elements from foreign policy analysis courses, that is, by including themes such as the influence of domestic politics and non-political issues. It will begin with a contextualising historical overview and then briefly examine contributing factors that shape thinking and policy on India’s external relations before looking specifically at key relationships and important policy areas.

column6: Faith, Freedom, and the Constitution: Religion and Law in India
column22:
Faith, Freedom, and the Constitution: Religion and Law examines the relationship between religion and law in contemporary India through the constitutional governance of religious diversity. It explores how courts, legislatures, and administrative institutions define religion, protect religious freedom, regulate religious practices, and adjudicate conflicts involving equality, citizenship, caste, and religious identity. While centred on India, the course adopts a comparative perspective by engaging debates from the United States and Europe concerning secularism, religious liberty, legal pluralism, and minority rights.
Organised around four foundational questions that have shaped some of the most significant constitutional controversies in modern India, the course first asks, under the theme of secularism: How should a constitutional state govern religion? It then examines, through the lens of religious freedom: What protections should individuals and communities enjoy? Turning to personal law and legal pluralism, it considers: Can religious diversity coexist with equal citizenship? Finally, through the study of caste and conversion, it investigates: How does law regulate religious identity and social hierarchy?
Drawing on constitutional texts, judicial decisions, and interdisciplinary scholarship from law, political theory, history, sociology, and religious studies, the course encourages critical reflection on the challenges of governing religious diversity in democratic societies. Particular attention is paid to the ways in which constitutional commitments to liberty, equality, secularism, and minority protection intersect—and at times come into tension—in contemporary legal and political debates.

"Why are the young women of some communities of Tamil Nadu, for example, expected to marry their maternal uncle i.e. mama? How and why did the Kulin Brahmins of Bengal justify having numerous wives? Traditionally, amongst the Nair, women were financially independent and inherited their mother’s house. Why did British colonialism change certain laws around marriage and inheritance and how did these transform family structures as well as ideas of gender and community in South Asia? Kinship, or how people are related to each other, has been an important way of learning about them and their culture. The categories some of us might have long considered “natural” such as gendered identities, patriarchal norms, social hierarchies, and even political systems, have revealed, especially when considered in light of other cultural systems, as constructed. So when discussing the Nair kinship system or hijra understandings of identity and community, for example, we will explore the role of religion and colonialism to critique traditionally held Western notions as well as deeply engrained religious beliefs, both centring on the patriarchal family and its associated gender essentialisms. 
A close study of kinship patterns from across the world will throw up historically variable, socially produced, and politically charged issues, which will enable us to critically explore the blinkered beliefs held on race, caste, and gender. After briefly situating the anthropological debates on kinship, gender, relatedness, caste, and community, this course will introduce a range of contemporary ethnographies to discuss recent socio-legal and political developments and how these end up refashioning today’s societal norms."

column6: Introduction to Feminist Theory (Formerly known as "Gender, Culture and Politics: Feminist Thought and Practices-SOCL206|POLT215")
column22: This course introduces key directions and themes in feminist thought and practice, both global and local, spanning a time frame starting from the eighteenth century to the contemporary times. Examining how gender and sexuality operates in society, we examine how gender is not an individual attribute or a role, but rather a system of social practices that constructs different categories of people—“men” and “women”—and organizes social interaction and inequality around this difference. The course will take a sociological approach in understanding what is sex and gender , how they operate in the labor market, at home, and at school, and how they structure our everyday lives at the individual, interactional, and institutional level. Throughout the course, we will prioritize reading, evaluating, and questioning feminist theory and sociological research on gender. We will also investigate feminist thought from a variety of disciplinary perspectives and theoretical orientations and focus on key debates such as the sex/gender system, intersectionality, sexual difference, and essentialism, amongst others. This course aims to think through the ways in which gender and sexuality intersect with caste, class, community and the nation. The aim of this course is to unravel the centrality of power in the practice of gender.

column6: Quantitative Research Methods in Humanities and Social Sciences
column22: This course will introduce students to quantitative methods for social sciences. This is designed as a foundational course for those interested in research in social sciences. It is meant to amiliarize students with modern statistical methods and their applications to research in social sciences.

Why does media ownership matter? Is media freedom genuinely safeguarded in democracies, or is that merely a myth? How does social media contribute to community polarization in India? What constitutes the public sphere, and to what extent is it shaped by gender? How do diasporic communities negotiate cultural identity through food and engage in political discourse via social media? In what ways do diasporic communities engage with social media for political participation, debate and mobilization, and how does this impact political dynamics in both their host and home countries ? This course seeks to critically examine these pressing questions by engaging with key theoretical and empirical scholarship at the intersection of media, politics, society, and diaspora. It will provide participants with conceptual tools to analyze how media practices are shaped by power relations, and how they, in turn, influence public life, and shape up identity. The course concludes with a project, allowing participants to apply core concepts and analytical frameworks to contemporary empirical media related issues or case studies. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, interdisciplinary engagement, and reflexive analysis.

Why does media ownership matter? Is media freedom genuinely safeguarded in democracies, or is that merely a myth? How does social media contribute to community polarization in India? What constitutes the public sphere, and to what extent is it shaped by gender? How do diasporic communities negotiate cultural identity through food and engage in political discourse via social media? In what ways do diasporic communities engage with social media for political participation, debate and mobilization, and how does this impact political dynamics in both their host and home countries ? The course concludes with a project, allowing participants to apply core concepts and analytical frameworks to contemporary empirical media related issues or case studies. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, interdisciplinary engagement, and reflexive analysis.

‘The more data the better’! ‘Data is the new oil’! This course problematizes these maxims by familiarizing students with the politics and paradox of data in healthcare. The course examines how data is produced, enacted, cleaned, refined, represented and utilized to diagnose and prevent disease outbreaks, expand access to healthcare, and determine patterns of funding and resource allocation in global health. In recent years, the term data has been attached to a range of approaches and processes, such as data-driven, data-fied, and data-based systems, to signify the promises that data holds for improving healthcare and advancing development.
Central to these approaches are the infrastructures and technologies (digital and otherwise), such as surveys, statistics, satellites, smartphones, apps, algorithms, big data, platforms, and artificial intelligence, that generate, maintain and circulate data from dispersed sites in the pursuit of more precise, predictive, and pre-emptive health outcomes. We ask how these infrastructures reconfigure everyday health work, doctor-patient relationships, and broader understandings of expertise, innovation, accountability, transparency and trust. And, on a more micro level, how digital and data infrastructures encourage new forms of self-care and self-monitoring practices? 
What modes of health governance do data infrastructures enable and what does that tell us about the role of the state in the delivery of healthcare? What happens when an eclectic mix of new public-private actors (technologists, designers, entrepreneurs, and consultants) enter this ecosystem? And, what does that reveal about underlying power dynamics, inequalities and market interests that animate data-driven healthcare? This course brings together scholarship from science and technology studies, medical and political anthropology, and critical data studies. We will read ethnographic accounts (with a significant focus on India and Africa) as well as policy-oriented documents. This approach situates grounded, empirical insights within broader political and institutional contexts.

column6: Gender, Masculinity and the Languages of Grief
column22: This course explores grief as a political emotion and examines how gender is constituted in response to loss. Using a range of texts that draw upon literature, psychoanalysis, and anthropology—including traditions of lament and dirges across cultures, as well as ancient and modern literature on grief, and explorations of gendered modes of grief historically available to men and women—it offers insights into how men and women are socially expected to process loss and perform mourning. The course invites reflection on how such performances, both in everyday and eventful contexts, whether aligned with or at variance with social expectations, enable the articulation of divergent political imaginaries and possible futures that could potentially disrupt the dominant order of things.

column6: Modern day Storytelling: An introduction to documentary filmmaking and its use in peoples and environmental movements
column22:
Documentary films are modern, technology driven storytelling. A medium that can turn anyone’s life and its stories into interesting visual narrations. This course follows the journey of the camera from being a tool that exudes aesthetics, creativity, and capturing of memories, to becoming the strongest instrument of resistance in the struggles of ordinary people. Through a series of interactive lectures the students will explore how the medium of documentary filmmaking can bring stories that are invisibilised, to light. 
At the core of documentary filmmaking lies the critical concept of integrity, the ability to visually capture stories of people and the world just as we see it. Hence, this course will allow students to not only immerse themselves in historicity, but also develop ethics in practice.

column6: Jaalis: Cutting through from the Past to the Present
column22:
The cut work windows, or “jaalis”, as an aesthetic as well as a practical architectural feature, has been used in multiple cultures through history, typically in hot and arid places. This was most famously used, and most well-crafted (in stone), during the Mughal era. Jaalis have been made in wood, stone, ceramics, and even, (rarely), in metal.
 In this ceramics course, we will touch upon all of them and their histories, but concentrate mostly on the designing and making of terracotta clay jaalis. Students will study the history of jaalis and then go through the process of sketching patterns inspired by what they see around them, on campus, to develop and execute your own modular jaali design.

column22:
In an increasingly digital and online world we are losing touch with the physical, tactile world around us and the act of creating with our own two hands. Existing creative pursuits are turning digital and the opportunity to engage in tactile craft practices, creating using physical tools and materials, is increasingly rare. 

 This course introduces students to techniques of crafting and expressing creatively using a variety of tactile materials, and gives them the opportunity to learn a hands-on skill.
 All students will have introductory sessions of basic drawing, colour theory, colour mixing, printing, paper manipulation, clay work, yarn, fibre, simple looms, fabric, sewing, dyeing, and using found materials.

 They will then each pick one of these mediums to explore in depth and undertake disciplined practice of, while situating it in a historical and traditional context.
 
 There may be a field trip too.

column6: Arts of the Deccan: The Early Modern Epoch from Vijayanagara to the Marathas
column22:
In understanding the history of Indian arts, knowing the Deccan, its place and role, is crucial. In this course we will travel the triangular realm of “Dachinabades” as named in the first-century Periplus of Erythraean Sea, exploring its contours through the lens of its artistic traditions, literatures and cultures. Since this exploration will become very ambitious if we were to cover all aspects of Dakhina (Prakrit) arts, we narrow it down to the Early Modern Period (fifteenth-century onwards), a momentous time of which we have an immediate cultural memory, making the study of artistic heritages a traceable historicity. We will study the Deccan’s unique art forms and cultural practices through music, dance, literature, architecture, paintings, food and fabric that reflect the multicultural and cosmopolitan socio-political ambience in which rulers such as Krishnadevaraya, Adil Shah, Raghunatha Nayaka, and Serfoji each played significant roles. Through readings, viewings and other detailed digital archival material we will learn to close-watch performative arts of the early modern era as milestones in the cultural history of India. The aim of the course is to enable students identify the distinct features of each of kingdoms such as Vijayanagara, Sultanate, Nayaka and Maratha as well as to have a panoptic view of early modern era’s artistic legacies whose essence manifests in diverse cultural encounters. The course will prod us to think of deliberate omissions and censoring when the nation-state regrouped its artistic heritages.
 Coursework will include readings, class discussions-seminars and presentation style disseminations requiring high level of class participation, interactive assignments and some writing work. While the course does not demand any art practice background, those who are practitioners of any genre will be encouraged.

Course Objectives/ Outcomes
To introduce some of the artistic traditions across genres from the early modern era and help students learn/read the movement of art through its socio-political legacy
To work on aspects of embodiment, wherever possible to add value and inspiration to the course work
To interweave with the domain of history bringing a multi-perspective approach to political history and to challenge the dominant narratives in mainstream understanding about religious differences, peoples' tolerance towards each other and early movements of modernisation through the understanding of the arts of the Deccan world.

column6: Performance Practicum - “This is how we Perform Today”
column22:
The journey of performing traditions (dance, music and theatrical performances) into the 20th century is pregnant with its immediate cultural memory. This course will focus on embodied learnings of some of the traditions that have been altered because of the post-colonial censuring that led to a normative establishment of artistic traditions as “classical” and “folk”. Through the course, students will encounter art practices such as Lavani, Gujjili poetry, Karakattam/Kattai Koothu, Raaja paat or  Stri Paat theatre performance and Reality show performances. Through media- embodiment, we will gain foundational knowledge of these forms even as we draw attention to notions of “purity” and “honour” attached to artistic traditions that affect the way we have inherited them. The course uses corporeality in practice as a tool to encounter the socio-political and economic lives of the artistes who practice these arts.
The course does not require the student to have prior knowledge in any art form, but must be willing to participate in class practicums. Grading will be commensurate with willingness and enthusiasm to experiment and learn, rather than expertise in practice. This course is meant to offer further insights towards the Pathways in the Arts course by way of lending an experiential understanding of artistic traditions. The classes will be a mix of embodied learnings (music, dance and theatre forms), video footage viewings and some discussions on performative traditions.
Learning Outcome
Students will learn a range of performative forms, in practice
Students will learn to pause and analyse the nuances of technique in footwork, movements, dialogue delivery and rhythms in each section
They will develop a language of movements  and also learn of the history and politics of embodied performance

column6: Introduction to Literary Studies (previously Literary Methods)
column22: This course is designed to introduce Literature majors to some of the fundamental concepts and practices of literary criticism. We shall begin with a preliminary survey of the history of literary study as a way to propose working definitions of a few key terms: What do we mean by literature? What is a text? Who is an author? And what constitutes literary criticism? This last question will bring us to questions that pertain directly to method: In what ways can a text be read? Does it make sense to speak of a literary method in the same way as we speak, say, of the scientific method? Or, to put it another way, is there anything that all works of literary criticism share in common, or is it futile to look for such a common ground?

The Introduction to Creative Writing is an intensive writing workshop designed to give students the opportunity to develop their craft via in-class workshops, readings, discussions, and one-on-one tutorials. The discussions will also focus on publishing and the publishing industry. The course will include Zoom sessions with authors and literary agents. 

The class will mimic the frenzied pace of real-life publishing. There will be deadlines, drafts, and redrafts. We will learn to read like writers and write like writers under pressure. 

Students will turn in one fully realized piece of fiction (a short story or the first chapter of a novel in progress) and a book review for the course. For the book review, students will choose a work of fiction by an author who comes from a background different from theirs (we will discuss in class what this means) on which to write a paper and give a presentation. The paper will be divided into two sections – the first will be a 1,000-word review of the book, and the second will be an analysis of the reviews the book has garnered in the media. The analysis should include students’ thoughts on the audience the book was written for, the type of marketing that might have gone into the book, the cover, the hooks used to gain publicity, author interviews, etc. You will need to search The New York Times, New Yorker, Guardian, Washington Post, Hindustan Times, Hindu, Financial Times, and other publications for reviews and features on the book. You will give a 10-minute presentation on your review.

This course aims to introduce students to Translation Studies (TS), by engaging with specific questions central to the domain. These questions revolve around the concept of equivalence, including issues of equivalence at various levels of language and text; they relate to challenges specific to non-literary and literary translations. At the same time, this course exposes students to various theoretical perspectives on translation in its interactions with culture. Beginning with a broad outline of the scope, history and central issues of TS, this course goes on to discuss various levels of equivalence. It begins with a focus on non-literary translation, and, thereafter, opens up to challenges specific to literary translation. Beginning with a close-up view in order to engage with these ‘building blocks’ of translation, it then goes on to view the process of translation from its place within culture and addresses issues that flow from it. Finally, it brings up some philosophical perspectives on translation. Thus, the course aims to give a comprehensive view of the act of translation and of issues concerning the domain of TS.

column6: Android Dreams: Technological Imaginaries in Literature and Film
column22: We often hear that technology will solve our biggest problems—inequality, governance, even loneliness. But why has technology become the main way we imagine the future at all? And what kinds of futures does it make possible—or impossible? This course approaches these questions through literature and film. We will read short stories, speculative fiction, and literary texts alongside cinema, treating them not as entertainment or illustration, but as forms of thinking—ways in which societies imagine, desire, or resist technological change. Focusing on South Asia, we will explore technological imaginaries: how narratives give shape to ideas of progress, control, care, and the human. We will practice close reading and interpretation, paying attention to voice, form, metaphor, and narrative structure, and ask how stories make technological futures imaginable.

column6: Brief Encounters: The Short Story through Histories and Cultures
column22: If brevity is indeed the soul of wit, then the short story is the fictional equivalent of modernity: it captures an instant, a hovering mood, a passing shadow. In fact, in some ways the short story is the arch-genre of modernity. In the early to mid-19th century, the modern metropolis was being forged by capital, migration and anonymity; here rapid industrialisation made demands on uninterrupted time; the telegraph and the railways atomised distance; photography made visualising of a moment possible. It is in that kind of a city where print modernity took sharp turns and the short story became one of the founding genres to mirror the harried, hurried, fleeting life in the new metropolis. It came to belong to a space in between a sketch and a tale, a fable and a saga, an anecdote and a long narrative. This course would look at the cultural and social origin of the short story; enquire into the ways in which it has transformed over the last century and a half; look at some of the critical approaches to it; and study its astonishing fecundity and flourish, including in the Indian subcontinent. In short, this course will be a survey of the genre as well as one which would look closely at some of its most representative specimens, and in several languages.

Advanced Creative Writing is a twelve-week course in which students expand on the skills they acquired in Introduction to Creative Writing. You will master the elements of fiction via workshops, one-on-one tutorials and multiple rewrites. You will wax eloquent about plot and dialogue (did someone groan at “action beats”?). You will talk craft and lyricism and resolution. You will finesse your voice and form. You will birth compelling characters in well-thought-out settings. You will continue learning the rules of writing and break them with aplomb. This is a painfully intensive course. Be prepared for double the reading and writing you did in Introduction to Creative Writing. At the end of the term you will produce two fully realized short stories, which, the professor realizes, is difficult to accomplish in three months. You, the student, need to realize this, too, and embrace the chaos of real-life publishing. There will be innumerable drafts, redrafts and deadlines. Each draft you produce will be up for your peers’ consumption. You will all work as editors to help make a story the best it can be. Zoom meetings with practitioners of fiction, editors and agents will further your understanding of the publishing world.

column6: Cinema and the Idea of the Political
column22: This course looks at the critical moments of encounter between two defining intimations of public space — cinema and mass politics — without collapsing the autonomy of cinema as an art, and politics as an hermeneutic of collective self-determination. Cinema’s birth at the summit of industrial modernity is no news, and neither is its capacity for both mass enrichment and manipulation. But there is relentless and often renewed debate about ‘political cinema’ and its ‘uses’, which lead us to the very genesis of the idea of mass culture in the early years of modernity. It must be stated at the very onset that the course looks at ‘narrative cinema’ rather than on documentary, cinéma vérité, or at the visual cultures of Lettrists, Situationists, avant-gardists, surrealists etc., all of whom have done pioneering work in the domain. How did cinema capture the political zeitgeist of the 1920s, 1940s and 1960s? Or even after? On the other hand, how does politics - as a thought and practice - allow for cinematic/spectacular enunciation? Habermas scholar Robert Porter pointedly asks, “Does cinema express or engender political thought? Can we think of cinema, or certain specific cinematic texts, as bodies of political theory?” His is an assertive nod. As an undergraduate course, this one would not set the high ambitions of teaching political theory through cinema. Therefore, the course does not name itself ‘political cinema’. There are, if one could say so, as many political films as there are kinds of politics, but more importantly, unlike other ‘studio-defined’ and ‘market-refined’ genres like ‘horror’, ‘crime’, ‘musical’, and ‘social’, political cinema has remained notoriously undefined (and undefinable). The way Soviet Cinema was ‘political’ is not the way James Bond Cold War spoofs were, nor were the French or Czech New Wave; or say, Satyajit Ray’s political fables made for children. But they are all political in the wide sense of the term. Hence, this course would not like to begin with an apriori idea of ‘political cinema’ but rather inquire if such a conceptual framework emerges through and with the course. To that end, the course would follow in the steps of Walter Benjamin, the Frankfurt School, Third Cinema and its legacies, and postcolonial uses of cinema. Claire Molloy and Yannis Tzioumakis, in The Routledge Companion To Cinema And Politics says that cinema “remains central to the formation and transformation of geopolitical discourses, imagining new geographies and connecting (or separating), in complex ways, the concepts of boundaries and territories with ideas about nation and identity.” At the same time, cinema has often found expressing working class and feminist solidarity as much as it has bored into the pervasive and pernicious nature of political memory, politics as stimulus, and the abiding lust for tyranny in political regimes. These will be some of the lines of argument/reflection in this course.

column6: The Lives and Afterlives of Great Books
column22: New course description: "This course offers a foundation in literary studies, through the medium of great books, and their reception across time. Engaging questions of what constitutes a great book, canonization, intertextuality, and methods for reading, we will study some of the greatest and most influential works of literature in translation, adaptation, and discursive dialogue. This class is reading-intensive, and of particular importance to students in the humanistic disciplines. Each iteration of the course will focus on a single intellectual, literary or performance genealogy, be it through the centering of specific texts, or through specific concepts, genres, or media. In Trimester 1 of the 2026-27 academic year, students will close-read and interrogate the Greco-Roman Homeric intertextual canon, with the Iliad as our core text. All students must purchase physical copies of the required texts for the course, without exception, due to the annotative nature of assignments.

column21: Scientific Reasoning (KCCS121-SCR), Data Analytics (KCCS124-DAN), Mathematical Reasoning (KCCS102-MR)
column22: Based upon selected case studies, this course covers notions of scale from building blocks of life to biomes, organisational levels and integration of biological units, and the primacy of description. We start with Aristotelian classification and proceed through Early Modern natural philosophy and natural history to the discipline of biology itself in the present day. We consider the development of particular philosophies and forms of technology from the 17th to 19th centuries and corresponding development of elements of biology at different points in time, including such concepts as biogeography, ecology, evolution, cell biology, genetics, anatomy, and physiology, even as theological holds over the subject begin to waver.

column22: Chemistry for biologists: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of chemistry with an explicit focus on their relevance to biological systems. Topics are motivated by examples drawn from cell biology, physiology, biochemistry, and microbiology. Experimental demonstrations and in-class problem-solving exercises connect chemical principles to the phenomena students encounter in their biology courses. The course has been designed to give biology majors the quantitative and conceptual chemical foundation necessary for advanced study in biochemistry, molecular biology, microbiology, pharmacology, and biomedical research

column22: Physics for biologists: The course uses basic biophysical concepts and experimental illustrations to explaining the physical principles that govern biological systems at the molecular level. The course combines classroom teaching with discussion of scientific observations that concur with theories. The course also aims to illustrate how various biomolecules behave as outliers, allowing for modification of these theories while providing a biophysical explanation for their behavior.

column22: This course is an introduction to the principles that guide the multifarious processes in the cell at the molecular and cellular levels and is intended for a college level audience. The content is an answer to the question: What is the molecular basis of cellular structure and function? Concepts covered include the storage, transfer, and regulation of genetic information, the interactions between molecules, and their assembly and disassembly in cellular functions, the cytoskeleton and its role in cell and tissue shape, molecular traffic between the various cellular locations and across the membrane boundary, signaling within the cell and between cells, cellular metabolism, the cell-cycle, division, growth, development, differentiation and death, and the energy conversions that power all these processes. The course will focus more on principles than on encyclopedic detail, and will be linked to modules taught in earlier trimesters to enable comprehension.

column21: Life at Different Scales (BIOS201), Scientific Reasoning (KCCS121-SCR), Data Analytics (KCCS124-DAN)
column22: How did life first arise on Planet Earth 4 billion years ago? In this course, which comprises both organismal and molecular evolution, we will begin with early theories of evolution that lead up to Darwin and Wallace's theory of natural selection. We thus gain insight into the process of scientific inquiry that resulted in one of the most important theories in the biological sciences, before concluding by integrating it with Mendel's theory of genetics referred to as the Evolutionary Synthesis. The course will look at the evidence of macro and micro evolutionary processes, and the evolution of plants and animals to understand the basis of the diversity of living organisms on Earth. Through numerous examples, students will learn about adaptive strategies at the level of individual organisms that may underlie evolutionary changes at the level of a population. At a molecular level, we trace the evolution of life, starting from self-replicating molecules, to the RNA world, to the evolution of cellular components. Along the way we will discuss the role played by the constituent molecules of life. We will discuss the origin of the field of molecular genetics from the Evolutionary Synthesis, bringing the disparate fields of evolutionary biology and genetics together. We will discuss the development and employment of the molecular clock and the salience of neutral mutations in establishing relatedness among organisms, using such markers as mitochondrial, chloroplast, ribosomal and nuclear genetic material, aided considerably by such technological advancements as protein electrophoresis, leading to the amplification of DNA using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for whole genome sequencing. This course will briefly discuss how the sequence information comes together with the current computational power to draw the phylogenetic tree of life.

This course will begin with an overview of animal behaviour and how it has integrated concepts from many disciplines to advance the field. Next, animal behaviour will be studied from an evolutionary perspective before understanding the bases for the variation in behaviours within and among individuals, populations, and species. With these concepts in mind, a range of behaviours will be examined using case studies. Finally, more complex behaviours related to social interactions among animals will be considered.

column22: Bacteria are the most dominant forms of cellular life on earth. Their ability to adapt to the entire gamut of environments on our planet is coded somehow in their DNA. We will discuss how this fascinating kingdom of life adapts to its circumstances by studying the structure, organisation and evolution of their genomes. We will take a conceptual and computational approach towards these aims. A particular goal of this course will be to help students conceptualise, design and implement (at least in part) a mini-project analysing bacterial genomes.

column22: This course will discuss molecular aspects of gene regulation in bacteria. Gene regulation is fundamental to bacterial adaptation to their environments and is achieved by a complex network of regulatory proteins and their interactions with DNA. How this network functions and how it sustains bacterial life as we know it are the key themes this course will cover.

The course begins with introducing the plant’s meristem and its histological organization to the students, followed by the anatomy of the leaf and other simple & complex tissue structures and their organization. Water is important to plant life, and other mechanical phenomena happening inside plants, such as diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, imbibition, guttation, transpiration, etc., are considered. It introduces the stomata & the mechanism of opening & closing that enable gas exchange between plants and the atmosphere. Identifying the essentiality of nutrients is foregrounded, along with their roles, the mechanism of uptake of nutrients, and the mechanism of food transport within plants. What role does gravity play, and how will plants grow in space? We learn about concepts of photosynthesis and pigment systems/photosystems. Other important phenomena are discussed, such as photophosphorylation, the Calvin cycle and photorespiration in plants. Carbon fixation, indoor and otherwise. How pollution affects them etc. We consider how and why plants go under nitrogen metabolism, how molecular nitrogen fixation happens, and its significance to the world. Plants also need/use hormones for their growth and development. We discuss how growth hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, and ethylene work. We complete the circle by looking at the seed. We introduce students to seed dormancy, its germination, and the concept of photoperiodism and vernalization. We talk about genetically modified plants and seeds (GMOs) and the hazards and ethical issues around them. The genetic basis of the adaptations in plants and how they vary with the types of climates, for example, how do they become resilient to drought? A brief introduction to modern plant biotechnology and gardening is also discussed. Concept integration and awareness about ecosystems, global warming, forests and the plantation of trees

column6: Molecular Modelling and Simulations - A Quantum Chemistry Approach
column22: This advanced course provides an in-depth exploration of molecular modelling and simulations with a strong emphasis on quantum chemistry techniques. Students will gain theoretical knowledge and practical skills in using computational methods to investigate the properties and behavior of molecules. The course covers the principles of quantum mechanics as they apply to molecular systems and introduces various computational tools used in modern quantum chemistry.

column6: Molecular Modelling and Simulations - A Quantum Chemistry Approach
column22: This advanced course provides an in-depth exploration of molecular modelling and simulations with a strong emphasis on quantum chemistry techniques. Students will gain theoretical knowledge and practical skills in using computational methods to investigate the properties and behavior of molecules. The course covers the principles of quantum mechanics as they apply to molecular systems and introduces various computational tools used in modern quantum chemistry.

Molecules of Life introduces the fundamental biomolecules that form the basis of living systems. The course explores the structure and function of proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids. Students learn how these molecules interact to support cellular processes and metabolism. Emphasis is placed on the relationship between molecular structure and biological function. This course provides a foundation for understanding biochemistry and molecular biology in advanced studies.

column6: Discrete Mathematics (formerly: Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science I: Discrete Mathematics)
column22: Discrete Mathematics course will provide students with their first glimpse of how to think rigorously about discrete and finite phenomena. The course will begin by introducing students to the language and grammar of mathematics. It will then proceed to an axiomatic construction of the natural numbers, and introduce the fundamental mathematical notions of sets, relations, and functions. The remainder of the course will be organized around three distinct modules: number theory, permutations and counting, and graph theory.

This course offers a foundational understanding of essential programming methods, with a focus on their practical applications. The objective is to facilitate fluency in programming and the ability to switch between various programming languages. The course introduces fundamental algorithms and data structures, and how they can be used to solve computational problems or extract information about given data.
This course offers a foundational understanding of probability and statistics essential for study of randomized algorithms, modeling and data science.

column6: Software Design Practical (Formerly: Group Design Practical)
column22: This is a project based course that works towards students having built a complete application of their choosing from ground up, with guidance from instructors. Students will be introduced to programming methodologies and tools and processes (iterative approaches) that will help them with the task. They will also be introduced to the required architectural components and how they interface with each other. The human side of building such applications includes requirements gathering, basic user study, ethics issues and broadly “responsible engineering”.

What connects routing in computer networks to IPL player auctions? What connects dynamic pricing of flights to arms control negotiations? It turns out all of these scenarios are where there are sequences of decisions to be made. Decisions that are driven by some rationale: enhance efficiency of networks, get the best players at lowest price, sell all flights tickets at high prices, etc.
Game Theory is the mathematics of decision making that demystifies the complex logic of such interactions. It remains one of the most fundamental concepts in economics; in fact, multiple game theorists have won the Economics Nobel Prize, the most famous being perhaps John Nash.
With high-stakes trading and the rise of multi-agent AI, modern game theory has a particularly computational flavour, that requires not only a mathematical understanding of decision making, but also to compute those decisions quickly.
This course is designed for computer science students with an interest in real-world algorithms and economics students with an interest in the computational aspects of the subject. It will cover classical topics and then give an overview of modern trends.

column6: Autonomous Agents and Sequential Decision Making in AI
column22:
This course examines how autonomous computational systems observe, reason, learn, and act across increasingly complex environments. Structured around a unified “agentic systems” framework, the course introduces students to sequential decision-making through deterministic search, strategic planning, probabilistic reasoning, reinforcement learning, and modern tool-using AI agents. Rather than treating classical AI, reinforcement learning, and contemporary LLM-based systems as disconnected paradigms, the course presents them as successive architectural layers of intelligent agency. Students progressively construct computational agents that evolve from search-based solvers into adaptive systems capable of planning under uncertainty, learning from interaction, invoking external tools, maintaining memory, and operating within safety constraints.
Through an integrated practical lab structure, students maintain a cumulative software repository that is incrementally extended throughout the semester. By the end of the course, students will have designed and deployed a robust autonomous system that combines formal algorithmic rigor with contemporary AI engineering practices.
The course emphasizes durable conceptual architectures over transient frameworks, ensuring students understand the computational foundations underlying modern AI systems while remaining adaptable to future technological developments.

This course complements COMP308 with some extended topics – type systems and alternative application semantics. Understanding type systems is crucial for many modern programming languages and the course will develop that understanding (similar to COMP308) through implementation of a range of type systems and proving their soundness. Students will also be introduced to goal search as a programming paradigm with the associated concepts of unification and backtracking, with an introduction to Prolog. Lazy evaluation and implementation strategies for it will also be dealt with. The course will continue to use (Typed) Racket as in COMP308.

This 2-credit elective course bridges the gap between classic polynomial-time algorithms (COMP210) and advanced problem-solving paradigms required for computationally intensive optimization challenges of importance in the real-world.
The course introduces the notion of NP-completeness and then introduces paradigms for tackling NP-hard problems. The course focuses on foundational algorithmic problems such as Network Flows and Vertex Cover across multiple frameworks to give a cohesive understanding of how an algorithmic strategy shifts
depending on the computational constraints and desired solution accuracy.

This is a 2-credit; bridge elective course in programming; for students looking to pursue programming intensive disciplines. It helps students construct, think about, and work with computer programs as objects by
