column21: DATA201 (however removed in ERP to facilitate the registration)
column22: This course introduces the students to the field of data science and the kind of problems that can be solved by data science. Students will learn key data science skills, techniques, and concepts, including data analysis, statistical modelling, and some insight into some standard AI/ML algorithms. The course would also bring the perspectives of data from multiple branches of social sciences and provide a fundamental understanding of how data is conceptualized through the prism of humanities and social sciences. Further, the course will cover how data science skills can be used to address some of the vital problems in the field of social sciences. This would be done by a series of guest lectures by faculty members from social sciences. This is a hands-on course where after a quick primer on Python, the student will start with sourcing, processing, and cleaning a dataset. Then, use Python to mine data from its source and analyse available data by using NumPy and Pandas. Subsequently, the student will be introduced to modelling data to perform predictions using the SciPy, scikit-learn, and stats models libraries. In addition, the student will be introduced to visualization methods using the matplotlib and seaborn library to visually understand the patterns in the data. By the end of this course, students will be able to work on data science tasks practically with different Python libraries and achieve their goals.

This course will cover the following topics that are fundamental to the field of data science: Discrete Mathematics: logic, sets, functions, relations, mathematical induction, counting, recursion, trees, and graphs.Probability: axioms of probability; conditional probability and independence; random variables; continuous random variables and limit theorems.

column21: DATA205 (however removed in ERP to facilitate the registration)
column22: This course focuses on database system concepts and architectures, various data models, Database Design using ER models, UML, Relational Algebra etc. Database as well as web-based programming using SQL, PHP etc., will be covered. It also introduces theoretical concepts on database design and normalization, data storage with the corresponding file structures based on indexing using B-Trees, B+-Trees etc. Further, transaction processing and concurrency control principles will be introduced. Some applications on Information Retrieval and Data Warehousing will be covered.

column21: DATA202 (however removed in ERP to facilitate the registration)
column22: Recent advances in computing and information technologies, including hardware, software, databases, networks and communications have enabled the commercialization of many applications of Artificial Intelligence. Specifically, in the case of Supervised Learning, Deep Neural Networks and related algorithms have been able to achieve or even surpass human-like accuracy in applications like face recognition, voice recognition, automated driving, language translation, etc. This has given rise to multiple deployments of AI-based applications not only in the private sector but also in the Government. These deployments in areas such as recidivism prediction, algorithmic online ad targeting, drug addiction risk prediction, criminal intentionality detection in early stage shoplifting, etc. promise the effectiveness and efficiency of evidence-based decision-making. This early success has spurred rapid and frantic development of solutions using AI/ML and associated technologies without adequate safeguards and regulations. However, of late, multiple cases of bias and unfairness have been reported in the decisions made by AI/ML based algorithms, thus, raising ethical questions. In addition, AI/ML-based decisions cannot be explained easily due to their “black-box” nature. Impenetrability of AI/ML algorithmic decisions has reduced “trust” in the very algorithms that promised so much. This has spurred a call for Explainable AI (XAI) – AI-based decision-making that incorporates the notions of fairness, accountability and transparency.

Network science plays a crucial role in modern data science for modeling and analyzing
 relationships among complex systems. Graphs provide a powerful framework for
 representing and studying interactions across domains such as social networks, biological
 systems, brain connectivity, and technological networks. This course offers an applied
 introduction to graph-theoretic concepts and network science using Python.
 Students will learn how to represent data as networks and analyze their structural properties,
 including connectivity, paths, centrality measures, and clustering. The course further
 introduces network models such as random, small-world, and scale-free networks to
 understand real-world structures, along with community detection techniques to uncover
 hidden patterns within networks.
 Through hands-on exercises and case studies, students will construct and analyze networks,
 implement key algorithms, and interpret results in real-world contexts. The knowledge gained
 will support applications in areas such as social network analysis, biological and brain
 networks, graph-based machine learning, and data-driven decision-making systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is all around us. It‘s how Google answers our searches, Amazon recommends products, ChatGPT helps answer questions, and Spotify plays another song. Artificial Intelligence is changing the way decisions are being made in the world today. This course is intended to enable students to understand a critical aspect of AI, i.e., industry applications, scenarios, and use cases. The course covers this very critical aspect of AI, i.e., use cases of AI in a variety of industries such as Sales and Marketing, Retail Manufacturing, Healthcare, Education, to name a few.

column6: Tools and Methods in Environmental Studies
column22: This course will provide the basic vocabulary that students require to navigate the environmental sciences, humanities, and social sciences. Through systematic close readings of influential texts, we hope to enable students to use the tools and methods employed by these disciplines in the context of the environmental studies. We begin the course by charting out primary motivators and drivers of work in each discipline. We will then home in on cutting-edge research within each discipline. For example, in the environmental sciences, we will focus on the concept of thresholds and safe operating spaces for humanity. During our engagement with the environmental humanities, we will focus on how progress in the digital humanities has enabled visualisation and textual analysis of environmental history, philosophy, ethics, literary theory, art, and education. Lastly, in the environmental social sciences, we will pinpoint how ethnography and narratives are now becoming invaluable tools for understanding how society interacts with the environment.

column22:
Environmental studies encompass not only the science of climate change or environmental harm but also communicating these for various kinds of publics. 
 This course moves away from objective and expert accounts of environmental risk and policy to focus on popular and public-facing forms of environmental communication. 
 Students will read and analyse genres of Environmental Communication like science and nature writing and the photo essay. This course is writing-intensive and the focus will be producing various kinds of short written and visual pieces and forms of public outreach around case studies drawn from neighbouring ecosystems. As far as possible we will arrange student interaction with some practitioners of these forms.
 
 
 The theme for this year will be Water.

column22: Environmental science is the study of patterns and processes in the natural world and their modification by human activity. To understand current environmental problems, we need to consider physical, chemical and biological processes that are often the basis of those problems. This course will give you the skills necessary to address the environmental issues we are facing today by examining scientific principles and the application of those principles to natural systems. This course will survey some of the many environmental science topics at an introductory level, ultimately considering the sustainability of human activities on the planet.

column6: Environment versus Development: the policy dilemma
column22:
The growth versus environment debate has been one of India’s nay the global community’s major policy dilemmas for over a century now, exacerbated in the era of global warming and climate change. Further deepening the dilemma are the processes set off by globalization, privatization and liberalization combined with the role of technology in people’s lives.
 Yet, this debate has also spurred a new line of thinking and public policies in recent times.
 Growth is an imperative for material needs or poverty alleviation. But ecology, too, needs to be healthy, in the absence of which there’s a heavy price to be paid by the humanity, as witnessed in the unprecedented disasters: landslides, recurring floods and droughts, water scarcity or the devastation caused by extreme weather events and the society’s unpreparedness in such cases.
 It’s a quintessential “wicked problem” – to borrow from the term coined first in a 1973 paper by Horst W J Rittel and Melvin M Webber, professors of design and urban planning at the University of California at Berkeley (Dilemmas in a general theory of planning) – that does not allow for the best solution but rather only the acceptable compromises.
 Questions abound: Is there such thing called sustainable economic growth, as advocated by the different stakeholders? What’s the history and philosophy of environmentalism and the many different tensions centred around these two ideas? How does public policy factor in both?
 This course, drawing from field work and theoretical foundations, would offer students of social and environmental sciences with a keen interest in public policy a thorough review of this classical dilemma and the choices a society has and makes. 
 From the earliest debates over the construction of large dams, to industrial development, to the ideas of green economy or degrowth, and the history of India’s environmental legislation, the week-by-week sessions would build on the different thematic aspects of this debate and pose before students the confounding questions integral to understanding a public policy dilemma.
 For instance, the social and economic fallout of the land acquisition for development projects by the State using the whip of Eminent Domain: What happens to the people who are displaced by development projects? This itself posits several questions for consideration: Is development possible without any environmental, ecological or social harm? Or is there a need for a paradigm shift to strike a balance between the two processes, as the world runs out of time to deal with and eventually fix the global poly-crisis, a term coined by historian Adam Toonze.
 With class-rooms discussions intermittent with lectures, presentations and anecdotal stories from the field, this course will dwell upon the theoretical foundations as well as the real-life situations to explore tensions between the cause of environmental conservation and preservation and an inevitability of development for economic growth.
column24: The course will be mainly offered to ENVS students of the Third Year and Fourth Year as an Elective, but could also be opened up for economics and social sciences majors.

column22: Natural disasters are among the greatest threats for human lives and quality of life. This course introduces students to almost all the natural hazards that can cause disasters, from well-known frequently occurring ones to extremely rare ones. The course discusses the causes and consequences of natural hazards, efforts undertaken to predict them in advance and the complications of such efforts, in a fundamental level. The causes of natural disasters are understood based on the underlying scientific investigations. To predict them, routine measurement networks and scientific modelling are required. Finally, mitigating their effect depends on the support and efforts provided by the policy makers.

Materials have shaped history and our everyday lives. The social, political, and economic structures determining access to materials create varying environmental outcomes. Environment outcomes in turn shape societies and its practices over time via the provisioning of materials. Our current thinking about sustainability, conservation, and environmental crises are all largely shaped by the ramifications of our material relationships. While philosophers have expounded on the dialectic tensions between the material and the ideal as an intrinsic feature of the human condition for a long time now, only relatively recently have the implications of this dialectic tension been explored by scholars of the environmental studies to better understand environmental and social concerns, both of the present-day (overproduction, consumer culture, social-ecological fallout), and leading into the future (New Materialism).
 This course is designed to be a whirlwind tour of the various ways to think about environmental and social contexts underpinning various kinds of materialisms. Past and present cautionary tales of humanity’s precarious relationship with the material world ⎯the bedrock upon which the dialectic of the material and the ideal hinges on⎯ have culminated in ecological collapse and social strife. However, political, historical, and economic contexts complicate these simplistic cautionary tales to a large extent with regards to causality. Lastly, materials are what nourishes our body and our mind, and brings joy to our lives; we delight in the textures, noises, colours, and tastes of things. Discussions on future materialisms could be much less likely about how we value material things too much, but rather about how we don’t value them enough (Thorpe 2014).

column22:
Cryosphere is that part of earth that consists of snow (seasonal/permanent),
 glaciers, ice sheets, sea ice and permafrost. The cryosphere (especially ice sheets
 and glaciers) are responsible for lowering the heat budget of the earth by reflecting
 large portions of the incoming solar radiation as ice is a good reflector of radiation.
 Increasing global temperatures has led of reduction of the extent of the cryosphere in
 recent times. In this course, the students will be exposed to basic concepts and
 terminologies related to the field of climate-cryosphere interactions. In addition to
 that, the students will be asked to read and present simple research papers in this
 field with the guidance of the instructor.

column22: This course builds upon Analysis 1 and Analysis 2 by helping us generalise our understanding of notions like limits and continuity from sequences of real numbers and functions of a single real variable to more sophisticated contexts. The course begins by developing the theory of sequences of functions, and introduces the important notion of uniform convergence: continuity, differentiability, and integrability are studied in this context. This material is then used to better understand the role that polynomials play in spaces of functions and introduce the important idea of a power series.

column22: In this course, students will be introduced to the theory of rings and fields. The language of ring theory and field theory helps describe fundamental relationships between algebra, number theory and geometry and geometry, and provides a unifying framework for describing certain types of number systems and operator spaces.The course will begin with a study of important families of rings such as Euclidean domains, Principal Ideal Domains, and Unique Factorisation Domains. After a brief discussion of polynomial rings over Unique Factorisation Domains, the course will then develop the theory of fields. We will describe how to adjoin roots of polynomials to fields, and introduce the idea of an algebraic field extension. The course will conclude with a discussion on splitting fields.

column22:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the mathematical principles that underpin modern machine learning and data science. It is designed to equip students with the essential tools from linear algebra, calculus, probability, and optimization that are fundamental to understanding and developing machine learning algorithms.
  
 The course begins with vector spaces, matrix algebra, and linear transformations, emphasizing their role in representing and manipulating data. Key concepts such as eigenvalues, eigenvectors, orthogonality, and matrix decompositions—including spectral decomposition and singular value decomposition (SVD)—are explored with applications to dimensionality reduction and data approximation.
 
 Building on this foundation, the course introduces core machine learning techniques such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), regression models, and classification methods. Students will also study least squares approximation, model evaluation metrics, and the mathematical structure behind widely used algorithms.
 The course further develops essential tools from calculus, including gradients, Jacobians, and the chain rule, which are crucial for optimization in machine learning. Concepts from convex analysis and numerical optimization, including gradient descent and its variants, are introduced and implemented computationally. A review of probability theory is provided, leading to their applications in statistical learning and classification models such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs). Advanced topics such as duality, Lagrangian methods, and kernel-based classification are also discussed.

column6: Classical Physics: Energy and Force I
column22: Dynamics is the study of the response of objects to applied forces. Motion has been a subject of philosophical investigations since the time of Aristotle. It took a very long time before its foundations were laid during the 18th century. In the process, the subject of calculus was formulated as the then existing mathematical framework was inadequate to succinctly express the empirical observations. Newton, who finally formalized the required notions to describe dynamics, encoded the known observations in three laws that bear his name. Two major themes that underlie the conceptual framework of dynamics are force and energy. Later developments proved Newton’s laws to be inaccurate at high speeds and small distances. How approximate are they? Landing on Mars at any specified location still relies on the predictions made using these laws. For many of our endeavours in science and engineering, these laws are fantastically accurate. An understanding of dynamics is essential to pursue any of the specialized topics in physics. Classical dynamics is possibly the beginning of both physics and mathematical analysis. Nevertheless, it continues to inspire new ideas in both subjects.

One cannot imagine the modern world without the impact of electrical and electronic devices. This course will start with a discussion of the basics of electrical circuits, both static and transient. The main course content is centered around the theory of electronic devices based on semiconductors, such as P-N junction diodes and transistors. A study of these basic devices and their applications gives us the necessary background to design advanced circuits. Finally, the course will introduce the basics of digital electronics, covering Boolean algebra and logic gates.

Physics describes nature using particles and waves as basic entities. Newton's laws
 of motion govern the dynamics of particles. Sound, ripples on water, etc. are
 undulations of the medium in which they propagate. These waves arise due to
 interactions among the particles of the medium. Equations governing them are
 derivable from the laws of dynamics of particles. But electromagnetic waves do not
 require a medium for their propagation. Despite such fundamental differences,
 these waves are describable by the same mathematical structure. Physics students
 need a good grasp of these ideas since the concept of waves appears in many
 contexts such as the wavefunctions in quantum theory, the phonon modes in
 condensed matter, etc. This course presents the relevant physics and the
 mathematical details required to understand the subject.
column24: PHYS221 (recommended) for registering for this course

column22: The properties of electric and magnetic fields in material media allow us to understand polarization and magnetization of materials. These have tremendous applications in the form of microwaves and electromagnets, and are useful in explaining various chemical phenomena. On the theoretical side, the work of Faraday, Maxwell and others laid the foundation for the first major ‘unification’ of forces in the history of physics – the modern theory of electromagnetism. The behaviour of electromagnetic radiation (light) emerges naturally from this theory, giving us the laws of classical optics. The fundamental incompatibility of electromagnetic theory with Newton’s mechanics was what led Einstein to his special theory of relativity.

Light, being the medium of most observations and measurements, is our window to the physical universe. In this course, we study geometrical optics, where light is described by rays. This deals with basic components like lenses, mirrors and prisms, from which instruments like telescopes and microscopes are built. In addition, we study the wave properties of light at an introductory level. It includes phenomena such as light interference that accounts for the colours on soap bubbles and has applications ranging from quantum studies to gravitational wave detection. We will also study polarization, which is of importance in photography. In addition, we will discuss diffraction, which is used extensively to study the crystal structure of solids.

Newtonian mechanics is deterministic and applies to a system
 with many degrees of freedom. However, propagating a typical initial condition of the
 many-body system as per the Newtonian dynamical laws is fraught with difficulties,
 both conceptual and analytical. Luckily, if we are interested in a class of macroscopic
 properties which correspond to a myriad of microscopic states of the system, one can
 profitably employ the language of probabilities. Statistical physics of systems
 thermodynamic equilibrium is such a description. A major success of statistical physics
 is it provides a dynamical origin to the laws of thermodynamics, though for a restricted
 class of systems called ergodic systems. The theory, nevertheless, is applicable to all
 systems, microscopic and macroscopic systems included. This course is an introduction
 to some of the research questions in statistical physics. Specifically, the course deals
 with order theorems, critical phenomena and scaling theory.

column22: Every student of physics, irrespective of whether they wish to pursue theoretical physics or experimental physics, needs a thorough training in the core principles and conceptual structure of physics. The exposure should bring out the coherence and structure in the theories that shape our understanding of nature at all length and time scales. This course is an advanced overview of the discipline that teaches the language of physics as it is practised at advanced levels. This course will enrich and enable students so that they see experiments not as data generating endeavour but as the only way to uncover the deeper principles that seem to be at work in nature.

Physics is an empirical science. Its conceptual framework is revised to accommodate new empirical evidence from experiments. One of the earliest indications for the need to relook at classical physics was the blackbody emission spectrum. The experimental results were at variance with the prediction of classical physics. Max Planck proposed quantized exchanges of energy between the walls of the blackbody and the radiation within. This resolved the discrepancy between the theoretical predictions and the experimental observations. Einstein proposed quantized energy for the radiation field to explain the photoelectric effect. Bohr proposed non-radiating orbits for electrons to account for the stability of atoms and quantized angular momentum to explain their emissions spectra. All these ad hoc procedures found natural explanations in the quantum theory formulated by Heisenberg and Schrodinger. Their ideas were refined and put on firm scientific footing by Dirac, Pauli, Born, von Neumann, Jordan and others.

There is plenty of room at the bottom” is a succinct expression by Feynman about the richness of the quantum world. How do we harness this abundance? In this course, we attempt to answer this question. Peter Shor designing a quantum search algorithm that is much faster than any known classical algorithm marked the beginning of a new paradigm. The most relevant aspect is the way we process information. Doing it the quantum way speeds up the process, makes it more efficient and surpasses, in many cases, the limits known from a classical perspective. This course begins with a discussion on information theory and introduces ideas about quantum information processing (QIP). Other topics to be covered include quantum algorithms and their experimental implementations. Students will learn to program the IBM quantum computer as well. Major corporates in IT and many leading institutes have strong research programs in QIP. That vouches for the importance of this science.

Plato said, “Are you unaware that the true astronomer must be a person of great wisdom?”
 Twenty-four centuries later, our understanding of the universe is vastly better but still
 incomplete. This course on introductory astronomy and astrophysics will introduce
 students to the basic ideas and vocabulary of modern astronomy. The course will discuss
 observational methods of astronomy while giving students a chance to engage in taking
 quantitative data in practical sessions. This course acts as a gateway to the other two
 courses in the Astronomy track which will cover astronomical bodies, phenomena, and
 the overall structure of the universe.

Quantum theory is changing information processing in fundamental ways. At the root of this revolutionary change are superstition, entanglement and exponentially large size of the state space of multipartite quantum systems. These features are nonexistent in classical systems, and therefore, (classical) mechanical models of computation such Turing or Post machines have limitations. Quantum Information Processing (QIP) offers computational advantages and exponential speed up. The most fundamental element needed to harness these advantages is a
quantum bit (qubit, in short) array. In this course, we introduce quantum theoretic notions using
qubit as a protype quantum system. This allows us to quickly acquire enough skills to explore the
theory and its ramifications that form the basis of QIP

column22: This course offers a broad introduction to psychology as a scientific discipline. We will explore foundational topics such as perception, learning, memory, intelligence, motivation, emotion, and personality, and consider how these concepts help us understand everyday behaviour. We will also look at critical and contemporary perspectives that question how psychological knowledge is produced and whose experiences it represents. Across the term, you will read classic and contemporary research, connect theories to real-life examples, and practice communicating psychological ideas clearly in writing.

This course examines the biological basis of behaviour and develops an understanding of the complexities of the brain and the mechanisms underlying various behavioural phenomena. How is our brain organised? How do neurons function? What is the brain's basis of psychological phenomena? How do our genes and hormones influence behaviour? We will be exploring answers to these questions through interactive lectures. This course introduces brain disorders as a clinical method to better comprehend the complexity of the mind-brain connection. In addition, we will discuss various techniques such as brain imaging and recording and how they unravel the mysteries of the brain. By integrating knowledge from biology and psychology, students gain a holistic understanding of how biological processes shape human behaviour and cognition. This course is designed to provide an introduction to the major concepts, theories, and methods in the field of behavioural neuroscience.

The course examines changes across different time points in development by addressing four central questions of developmental science: continuity, plasticity, sources of development, and individual differences across the lifespan. Empirical data from infants, children, and adolescents will be examined to explain the developmental processes and learn about the emergence of the human mind.

column21: PSYC201 and PSYC208 and PSYC210 and PSYC211
column22: This course is attuned to the art of writing from a psychological perspective. It will commence by establishing the intrinsic connection between reading scientific texts and crafting them, providing students with insights into reading and interpreting various types of text, such as research papers, science journalism, and fiction. Subsequently, it will delve into the intricacies of articulating the challenging and often elusive facets of human experience that defy straightforward expression, and yet are the work of the psychological researcher. Addressing both abstract concepts and technical elements of scientific writing, students will engage in theoretical discussions, practical exercises, and real-world examples of writing on psychological topics. The primary focus will be on enhancing skills for writing research reports and research papers, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of effective writing principles within the discipline.

column6: Statistics & Research Methods I (Formerly know as "Statistics for Psychologists")
column22:
“Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.”
-Dr. Carl Sagan, astronomer, 1934-1996
What factors determine student grades? What is the correlation between student attendance and grades? Does breakfast improve attention? The answer to these questions is not factual but requires evidence, which involves gathering data from a sample and then synthesising the information using a relevant statistic to draw conclusions. We leverage statistical tools and techniques to gather evidence. This course provides an overview of the research process, including the use of scientific methods, research designs, and the role of theory in psychological research. Students will further gain hands-on experience in analysing real data using statistical analysis like measures of central tendency, t-statistics, ANOVAs & correlations.
Students will learn the basics of between-subjects and within-subjects design, as well as descriptive statistics, including measures of central tendency and dispersion. They will also explore surveys, such as probability, scales, and their uses, and learn about ANOVA. The course exercises will rely on hands-on exercises using statistical packages to explore, visualise and analyse these data. Students will delve into hypothesis testing, probability theory, and the concept of statistical significance. Further, they will learn about various sampling methods, considerations of sampling biases, and the complexities of generalising research findings to broader populations. A student emerging from this course will not only be equipped to use these tools and apply them, but also evaluate any ‘scientific evidence’ critically and judiciously. The students will learn to report and present data in a meaningful way and transform it into different visualisation formats, demonstrating an understanding of experimental design. This course provides the foundation for Statistics and Research Methods II (PSYC 209).

This course is designed to introduce students to theories in Counselling. Along with the emergence of Psychology as a discipline that was studying the human mind, Counselling as a practice was also emerging. Through Counselling, Psychology was offering the ways and means to work with human beings in psychological distress. Within Psychology, Counselling is the field that not only offers an application of various understandings of the mind, but also an important purpose to the vast knowledge that it generates. The history of counselling is rich and dynamic. It has been influenced by social, political and intellectual movements at various times. This course aims to familiarize the students with this complex past and present of counselling through some of the major theoretical streams that developed within Psychology.

Programming for Psychologists is an undergraduate course designed to equip psychology students with computational problem-solving skills. Through hands-on exercises in Python and Octave, students will learn to think like programmers, develop scripts to analyse behavioural data, run simulations, and automate research workflows. Emphasis on real-world applications includes data visualisation, statistical modelling, and research practices. The course also introduces LaTeX for creating professional reports and slides for effective presentations. By integrating coding fundamentals with psychological research methods, students will gain practical expertise in computational tools essential for advanced research, enhancing their ability to design experiments, manage datasets, and communicate findings efficiently.

column6: The Psychology of Sexuality and Gender
column22: This course introduces students to social, economic, and political dimensions of gender and sexuality with the goal of understanding how the diversity of these two aspects of the human experience impacts psychology and its allied disciplines. We will take a multi-disciplinary approach to explore, in particular: (i) differences and interrelationships between sex, gender, and sexuality; (ii) the relevance of cultural contexts to understanding human variation, especially as regards family, subjectivity, the politics of identification, and the impact of the predominance of ‘WEIRD’ research; (iii) theories of the performative aspects of gender and sexuality and the relevance of labour to gender and sexual roles and identifications; (iv) problems of categorisation and classification of normalcy and pathology, contemporary views on variation in biology, and the historical legacies of pathologisation of women and gender and sexual minorities; (v) problems in the public circulation and communication of specialist research (including overgeneralisation and misrepresentation of scientific findings and clinical practice); and (vi) some contemporary approaches in psychology research and practice that build on these social understandings. Students will gain experience in understanding how gender and sexuality are operationalised in psychology and its related fields of psychiatry and social work in both research and practice, as well as the tools to critically evaluate the promises and limitations of individual research studies by considering them in these broader contexts.

This course is designed to provide an introduction to psychotherapy skills. Students will be able to understand elements of ethical and effective counselling practice. They will be able to identify and use various helping Skills at a beginner level with an appreciation of personal and sociocultural factors. The course also aims to enhance students' understanding of self as a tool and increase self-awareness and self-reflective abilities. Students will practice helping skills with each other every week. Attendance is mandatory and contributes to the course grade. Note that the course will involve discussing and working with emotionally charged content. Students should also be prepared to reflect on and talk about (not mandated) some personal/emotional issues in class. 
Important Note: Completing this course does NOT qualify students to practice as counsellors or therapists.

Political psychology has been defined as the 'application of what is known about human psychology to the study of politics' (Sears, Huddy & Jervis, 2003, p. 3) and social psychology has influenced the study of political psychology more than any other subfield of Psychology. The course will introduce students to an overview of political psychology with a focus on questions that are currently central to the field’s concerns. These include construction of group identities, emotions and actions, collective mobilisation with a focus on leadership processes, and citizenship (as an example of group membership in a political community) through the lens of psychological theories. I have designed the course with learning built in three phases:
The first phase: will be bringing our common sensical understanding/ opinions/ knowledge/ to the table. We shall collate and think about what we ‘know’ about prejudice, for instance.
The second phase: we shall then interrogate our findings from phase 1 with research from psychological theories. I will lead this with lectures and working with our interactions in class as data points.
In the third phase, we shall work with the theories that we have learned to look at political material including websites/ speeches/ songs/ videos/ social media posts.
Students will thinking with psychological theories and the clarification of many misunderstood psychological studies (including the famous Obedience studies of Milgram, Conformity studies by Asch, and even the supposed bystander effect of not helping people in crisis.) Students of psychology will find that a healthy interest in the world around them, engaged thinking of stepping outside the realm of only the ‘individual’ will help in constituting the psychological selves in political ways.

This course introduces clinical psychology as a field concerned with understanding psychological distress within its broader social, cultural, and ethical contexts. It examines how concepts such as mental health, illness, and psychopathology are shaped by historical developments, theoretical frameworks, and systems of classification. Moving beyond purely individual explanations, the course foregrounds the role of social structures and lived experience in shaping mental health, with particular attention to the Indian context. It encourages students to critically engage with how distress is defined, interpreted, and addressed across diverse settings. Overall, the course positions clinical psychology as both a scientific and socially embedded practice, emphasising reflexive, context-sensitive, and ethically informed approaches to mental health and care.

In this course, we will learn about the developmental origins, progression, and social contexts of psychological disorders. Taking an integrative approach, this course draws upon developmental psychopathology, lived experience, and cultural perspectives to analyze what gets classified as psychopathology in childhood and adolescence. Case studies will be used to discuss how early developmental experiences shape mental health outcomes in adulthood and later life, and what risk and protective factors influence the nature of psychological vulnerability and resilience.

This course explores the development of the counselor’s personal and professional identities, focusing on the cultivation of self-reflection as a core clinical competency. Students will investigate the "person of the therapist" and how their own internal landscape — values, biases, family-of-origin patterns, and physiological states — influences the therapeutic encounter. Alongside this self-inquiry, students will practice and refine foundational counseling skills, including active listening, empathic responding and purposeful communication, recognizing that technical competence and self-awareness are mutually reinforcing dimensions of effective clinical practice.

This course investigates the common factors across models of psychotherapy and counselling, prioritizing the shared mechanisms of change over school/model-specific techniques. Students will examine the essential elements of successful counseling relationships while critically evaluating the foundational dichotomies and theoretical debates that define the field. By exploring these core tensions, the course provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the diverse landscape of modern approaches to mental health.

This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the Marriage and Family Therapy (MFT) field, tracing its historical evolution from foundational roots to modern-day applications. The curriculum investigates the theoretical architecture of both classical and emerging models, equipping students to critically appraise their utility across diverse family structures. Beyond theory, the course emphasizes essential clinical skills in family therapy as well as the ethical complexities unique to systemic work.
